6Linear Market Maker / Limit Order.

For K>0K>0, consider the linear bonding function f⁡(x,y)≜K​x+yf(x,y)\triangleq Kx+y. Solving the pool value optimization (1),

x∗​(P)={L/Kif P<K,0if P≥K,y∗​(P)={0if P<K,Lif P≥K.x^{*}(P)=\begin{cases}L/K&\text{if $P<K$,}\\ 0&\text{if $P\geq K$,}\end{cases}\quad y^{*}(P)=\begin{cases}0&\text{if $P<K$,}\\ L&\text{if $P\geq K$.}\end{cases}

Hence, this pool can be viewed as similar to a resting limit order2525 25 While the linear market maker is statically identical to a resting limit order, observe that they are dynamically different. In particular, once the price level KK is crossed, in a traditional LOB, the limit order is filled and removed from the order book. With a linear market maker, the order remains in the pool at the same price and quantity, but with opposite direction. This merely refers to a superficial change of the default strategy after a trade execution. that is, depending on the relative value of the price PtP_{t} versus limit price KK, either an order to buy (if Pt≥KP_{t}\geq K) or an order to sell (if Pt<KP_{t}<K) up to L/KL/K units of the risky asset at price KK. In this case,

V⁡(P)=L​min⁡{P/K,1}.V(P)=L\min\left\{P/K,1\right\}.

Observe that V⁡(⋅)V(\cdot) does not satisfy the smoothness requirement of 1 Part 2: the first derivative is discontinuous at the limit price P=KP=K. Thus, the characterization of Lemma 2 does not apply.2626 26 Note that the pool value function remains concave and thus the pool value process is a super-martingale. Hence, from the Doob-Meyer decomposition, a non-negative monotonic running cost process (analogous to 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR}) exists. However, this process is not described by (7)–(8). Instead, it can be constructed using the concept of “local time” and the Itô-Tanaka-Meyer formula, but we will not pursue such a generalization here (Carr and Jarrow, 1990, see, e.g.,).

7 Empirical Analysis

We now bring our model to data, showing how to separate the ‘‘alpha-like’’ and ‘‘beta-like’’ components of LP 𝖯&𝖫\mathsf{P\&L} in practice. This allows us to answer a number of questions. First, how large are the alpha-like and beta-like components, respectively, in terms of their contribution to the variance of returns? Second, how sensitive are the results to the frequency at which we rebalance the AMM’s holdings? Third, as we rebalance at increasingly high frequencies, does the result converge to the ‘‘alpha-like’’ microstructural component of returns — fees minus adverse selection costs — as our model predicts?

7.1 Methodology

We bring the model to data using the WETH-USDC trading pair2727 27 “WETH”, or “wrapped ETH” is a variation of ETH that is compliant with the ERC-20 token standard. Conversion between the two is a straightforward operation with a minimal fixed cost. For our purposes, we will view ETH and WETH as equivalent. on Uniswap v2 for the period from August 1, 2021 to July 31, 2022. The value of the reserves of this pool over the period are shown in Figure 4. Details of the data sources we use, and how we measure various quantities, are described in Appendix C.

Repeating (13), we have

LP 𝖯&𝖫 t−∫0tx∗​(Ps)​d​Ps⏟market risk⏞hedged 𝖯&𝖫 =𝖥𝖤𝖤t−𝖫𝖵𝖱t⏟fees minus 𝖫𝖵𝖱 .\overbrace{\text{LP $\mathsf{P\&L}$ }_{t}-\underbrace{\int_{0}^{t}x^{*}(P_{s})\,dP_{s}}_{\textrm{market\ risk}}}^{\text{hedged $\mathsf{P\&L}$ }}=\underbrace{\mathsf{FEE}_{t}-\mathsf{LVR}_{t}}_{\text{fees minus $\mathsf{LVR}$ }}. (24)

The left side of (24) can be thought of as the 𝖯&𝖫\mathsf{P\&L} from a delta-hedged LP position: the 𝖯&𝖫\mathsf{P\&L} of the LP position, minus that of the rebalancing strategy. This quantity can be estimated empirically under very weak assumptions:

  • •

    We can approximate the integral in (24) using discrete rebalancing strategies; for a fixed interval length Δ\Delta, we define:

    RB 𝖯&𝖫t≜∑s=0,Δ,2​Δ,…tΔ​RB 𝖯&𝖫t,\text{RB\ $\mathsf{P\&L}_{t}$}\triangleq\sum_{s=0,\Delta,2\Delta,\ldots}^{t}\Delta\text{RB\ $\mathsf{P\&L}_{t}$}, (25)
    Δ​RB 𝖯&𝖫t≜xtR​B​(Pt+Δ​t−Pt).\Delta\text{RB\ $\mathsf{P\&L}_{t}$}\triangleq x^{RB}_{t}\left(P_{t+\Delta t}-P_{t}\right). (26)

    Here, xtR​Bx^{RB}_{t} is the quantity of the risky asset in the pool reserves at time tt. Mathematically, (25) is a Riemann sum approximation for rebalancing strategy profits. Economically, (25) can be thought of as the payoffs of a strategy which delta-hedges at market prices to match the AMM’s holdings at time intervals Δ\Delta. This strategy holds xtR​Bx^{RB}_{t} on the interval [t,t+Δt)[t,t+\Delta t), and thus makes dollar profits equal to the holdings times the change in prices Pt+Δ​t−PtP_{t+\Delta t}-P_{t} on this interval.

  • •

    We measure LP 𝖯&𝖫 t\text{LP $\mathsf{P\&L}$ }_{t}, as our model suggests, essentially as Pt​xt+ytP_{t}x_{t}+y_{t}, using the observed pool holdings xt,ytx_{t},y_{t} and the CEX price PtP_{t}. In practice, pool reserves adjust over time through ‘‘mints’’ and ‘‘burns’’ of LP positions; we value these mints and burns periodically to CEX prices. Details of these calculations are provided in Appendix C.

7.2 Empirical Results

Figure 5 shows the results of our analysis. In Figure 5(a), the pool_pnl series shows unhedged LP pool 𝖯&𝖫\mathsf{P\&L}. The pool’s value is fairly volatile: daily gains or losses of over $10 million USD (on a pool reserves whose value varies between $100\$100–$300\$300 million USD, cf. Figure 4) are common. However, the vast majority of this risk is simply market risk: the pool holds a long position in ETH, whose price is very volatile over the period we study (cf. Figure 6). The hedged_pnl series show the hedged 𝖯&𝖫\mathsf{P\&L} from (24), rebalancing over various frequencies. Visually, these series are so much smaller than the aggregate pool_pnl series that their fluctuations are almost invisible in Figure 5(a).

Figure 5(b) zooms in, focusing on the hedged 𝖯&𝖫\mathsf{P\&L}. All of these series are substantially less volatile than the unhedged 𝖯&𝖫\mathsf{P\&L}. This is quantified in the return statistics in Table 1. Quantitatively, the standard deviation of returns of 1-minute hedged 𝖯&𝖫\mathsf{P\&L} is less than 1% of the standard deviation of returns of the unhedged 𝖯&𝖫\mathsf{P\&L}; in variance terms, 0.009% of the variation in returns in unhedged 𝖯&𝖫\mathsf{P\&L} comes from fees and adverse selection, and the remaining 99.991% simply reflects ETH price movements.

As the rebalancing intervals, hedged LP 𝖯&𝖫\mathsf{P\&L} becomes increasingly more volatile, reflecting market risk accrued within intervals. This is consistent with Corollary 1, stating that the rebalancing strategy corresponds to the variance-minimizing projection of LP 𝖯&𝖫\mathsf{P\&L} on market risk: trading strategies which are increasingly coarse approximations to the rebalancing strategy thus leave increasing amounts of variance within the hedged LP time series.

In the lvh series of Figure 5 and Table 1, we consider a benchmark which holds ETH holdings at the start of the sample and never rebalances, corresponding to ‘‘impermanent loss’’ (cf. Section 8). The volatility of ‘‘impermanent loss’’ measure is of the same order of magnitude at the unhedged pool. This illustrates why ‘‘impermanent loss’’ fails to account for market risk exposures: it perfectly hedges market risk at the start of the time interval, but accrues market risk as prices and holdings move over time; the result is a series that is almost as polluted by market risk as raw LP 𝖯&𝖫\mathsf{P\&L}.

7.3 Testing the Theory

Our model implies that, as we approximate the profits of the rebalancing strategy increasingly well, the hedged 𝖯&𝖫\mathsf{P\&L} should converge not to zero, but to the ‘‘alpha-like’’, microstructural component of LP returns on the right side of (24): accrued fees minus accrued adverse-selection costs. We can test this prediction by directly measuring this series, and comparing it to high-frequency hedged LP returns. We directly observe 𝖥𝖤𝖤t\mathsf{FEE}_{t}, fees paid into the LP pool over any given time period.2828 28 Uniswap v2 also allows for assets to be borrowed for “flash loans” for a fee; however, in v2, these loans are accounted for as swaps, thus 𝖥𝖤𝖤t\mathsf{FEE}_{t} contains revenue from flash loans. We discuss this briefly in Section C.1. For 𝖫𝖵𝖱t\mathsf{LVR}_{t}, since Uniswap v2 is a constant-product CFMM, adverse selection losses have the particularly simple expression in (19) of Example 3,

𝖫𝖵𝖱t=∫0tσs28×V⁡(Ps)​𝑑s.\mathsf{LVR}_{t}=\int_{0}^{t}\frac{\sigma_{s}^{2}}{8}\times V(P_{s})\,ds. (27)

We estimate daily realized volatility using Binance prices, see Figure 6. We can then compute 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR} simply by plugging in realized daily volatility and pool value to a version of equation (27) that is discretized at a daily frequency.

Note that, empirically, we measure the total fees paid by all kinds of traders. This differs slightly from our model, where we assume arbitrage traders pay no fees. Practically, since fees are simply an increasing process which potentially compensates for 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR}, whether fees arise from noise trade or arbitrage trade does not substantially impact the returns on LP positions. If we assumed arbitrage traders paid trading fees in the model, this would decrease the amount of arbitrage: instead of prices on the CFMM moving immediately to match CEX prices at all times, prices would have to move more than fees in order for arbitrage trade to have nonnegative payoffs. The analysis of arbitrage profits in the presence of fees is the subject of follow-on work (Milionis et al., 2023a).

We plot fees minus 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR} as the fees_minus_lvr_pnl series in Figure 5. Fees minus 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR} in our model closely track the pattern of hedged LP 𝖯&𝖫\mathsf{P\&L}. We plot the difference between these series in Figure 7. Observe that the gap is smaller for more frequent rebalancing frequencies. In this way, fees minus 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR} is an approximate continuous time limit of hedged 𝖯&𝖫\mathsf{P\&L}, just as our model predicts.

This increases our confidence that subtracting the ‘‘beta-like’’ rebalancing strategy from LP 𝖯&𝖫\mathsf{P\&L} indeed leaves an ‘‘alpha-like’’ residual which reflects the contribution of microstructural forces to AMM LP returns. In practice, we recommend that empirical researchers primarily construct hedged LP 𝖯&𝖫\mathsf{P\&L} simply by subtracting the rebalancing strategy’s profits from observed LP 𝖯&𝖫\mathsf{P\&L}: directly subtracting the payoffs of the hedging strategy is more straightforward to interpret, and imposes less theoretical structure on the underlying data.

7.4 Implications for Empirical Analysis of AMM Returns

Figure 5 and Table 1 show that LP 𝖯&𝖫\mathsf{P\&L} consists almost overwhelmingly of the ‘‘beta-like’’ market risk component. This has important implications for empirical analyses of LP returns: if market risk is not explicitly removed from LP returns, any results will predominantly reflect market risk rather than microstructural effects.

Suppose a researcher wishes to study the determinants of LP 𝖯&𝖫\mathsf{P\&L}, and attempts to do so by regressing unhedged LP returns (or fixed-start-point ‘‘impermanent loss’’, which behaves similarly) on some xx-variable. The best-case scenario for the researcher is that market risk is pure noise, uncorrelated with xx-variables. OLS coefficient standard errors are proportional to the standard deviation of the regression residual; thus, even in this best case, using unhedged LP returns as the y-variable leads to standard errors roughly 108 times larger than if hedged returns were used. Since standard errors scale with the inverse square root of sample size, achieving equal coefficient standard errors using unhedged LP returns as a yy-variable would require around 1082=11,664108^{2}=11{,}664 times more data.

In reality, a more severe concern is that market risk may be correlated with any xx-variables used. The large relative variance of market risk implies that even a weak correlation between the xx-variable and market risk can induce substantial omitted-variable bias, easily swamping any genuine relationship between xx and hedged LP returns.

We therefore recommend that empirical researchers analyzing AMM LP returns implement our results by using hedged LP returns as regression inputs. Our procedure has very low data requirements: to construct profits of the rebalancing strategy, (26), the researcher only needs xtR​Bx_{t}^{RB}, the time series of risky asset holdings of the CFMM LP, and PtP_{t}, the CEX price of the risky asset. Our results also appear robust to the choice of rebalancing frequency. Failing to hedge can have severe consequences: in empirical designs using unhedged LP returns, any microstructural ‘‘signal’’ — in our model, fees minus adverse selection costs — is likely to be overwhelmed by market noise.

A trader attempting to delta-hedge LP returns in practice would of course face various implementation costs, such as spreads and fees for rebalancing trades, or margin costs for maintaining a short position in the risky asset. Our goal here is not to precisely estimate the practical profits from hedged LP-ing; rather, it is mainly to conceptually decompose profits into market risk and residual components, analogous to alpha-beta decompositions in asset-pricing factor models. Following practice in this literature, we thus calculate RB 𝖯&𝖫t\mathsf{P\&L}_{t} assuming frictionless rebalancing.2929 29 While frictions of course play a role in practice, large trading firms have a variety of ways of optimizing these frictional costs; for example, they may rebalance at lower frequencies, optimize rebalancing execution, or “cross-hedge” by netting delta exposures across different parts of the portfolio, to limit trade and shorting costs. These practical factors imply that any attempt we make to quantify the frictional costs of rebalancing is unlikely to be generally accurate across all applied settings.

7.5 Markouts

Industry participants frequently use ‘‘markouts’’ as an approach to evaluate CFMM LP 𝖯&𝖫\mathsf{P\&L} (CrocSwap, 2022, see, e.g.,). Markouts, known as ‘‘realized spread’’ in the microstructure literature (Huang and Stoll, 1996), essentially attribute profits to trades by comparing the price of each trade to a future price, usually at some fixed time offset from the trade (e.g., 10 minutes) either from a CEX, or the CFMM itself. However, delta-hedging and the markout approach are in a sense closely related: the 𝖯&𝖫\mathsf{P\&L} of delta-hedged LPing, when rebalanced at discrete periods, turns out to be exactly equivalent to markout profits, marked to CEX prices at the end of discrete periods of the same frequency. In other words, the main difference between delta-hedging and markout analysis is whether the marking price is obtained in a fixed offset of time in the future after a trade, or based on the ending price of the interval the trade was contained in. These two are likely to be very close, especially when the markout offset or delta-hedging interval are short. Thus, delta-hedged LPing can be thought of as a microfoundation for markout-style analysis.

8 ‘‘Impermanent Loss’’

It is common in industry practice to evaluate LP 𝖯&𝖫\mathsf{P\&L} against simply holding the LP’s asset mix at some fixed start point; this is the loss metric we call ‘‘loss versus holding’’ (𝖫𝖵𝖧\mathsf{LVH}) in earlier sections, and is sometimes called ‘‘impermanent loss’’ in industry practice. In the notation of Section 5.2, defining the benchmark strategy xt𝖧𝖮𝖣𝖫≜x∗​(P0)x_{t}^{\mathsf{HODL}}\triangleq x^{*}(P_{0}), then 𝖫𝖵𝖧t≜𝖫𝖵𝖡t​(xt𝖧𝖮𝖣𝖫)\mathsf{LVH}_{t}\triangleq\mathsf{LVB}_{t}(x_{t}^{\mathsf{HODL}}) is defined as the loss process relative to this benchmark. Like 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR}, 𝖫𝖵𝖧\mathsf{LVH} has the property that it is non-negative, and can thus also be viewed as a ‘‘cost’’:

1.

For all t≥0t\geq 0, 𝖫𝖵𝖧t≥0\mathsf{LVH}_{t}\geq 0.

Proof.
𝖫𝖵𝖧t=R¯t​(x𝖧𝖮𝖣𝖫)−Vt=(Pt​x∗​(P0)+y∗​(P0))−(Pt​x∗​(Pt)+y∗​(Pt)),\mathsf{LVH}_{t}=\bar{R}_{t}(x^{\mathsf{HODL}})-V_{t}=\left(P_{t}x^{*}(P_{0})+y^{*}(P_{0})\right)-\left(P_{t}x^{*}(P_{t})+y^{*}(P_{t})\right),

and, by the optimality of Equation 1 for P=PtP=P_{t}, this quantity is always non-negative. ∎

𝖫𝖵𝖧\mathsf{LVH} seems like a simpler metric than 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR}, since it benchmarks profits to a single start point, and does not require calculating the profits of a continuously rebalanced benchmark portfolio. However, this seeming simplicity leads to severe problems with using 𝖫𝖵𝖧\mathsf{LVH} in practice.

8.1 Problems with Loss-Versus-Holding

First, 𝖫𝖵𝖧\mathsf{LVH} fails a basic ‘‘cumulation’’ property that is satisfied by most return-like metrics used in finance. Let 𝖫𝖵𝖧t,t~\mathsf{LVH}_{t,\tilde{t}} denote loss-versus-holding from tt to t~\tilde{t}, evaluated against buying and holding the time-tt portfolio. We have, in general:

𝖫𝖵𝖧t1,t2+𝖫𝖵𝖧t2,t3≠𝖫𝖵𝖧t1,t3\mathsf{LVH}_{t_{1},t_{2}}+\mathsf{LVH}_{t_{2},t_{3}}\neq\mathsf{LVH}_{t_{1},t_{3}} (28)

This non-additivity arises because 𝖫𝖵𝖧t2,t3\mathsf{LVH}_{t_{2},t_{3}} is benchmarked against time-t2t_{2} holdings, instead of time-t1t_{1} holdings. A simple example appears in the ‘‘reconvergence’’ paths PU​DP^{UD} and PD​UP^{DU} on Figure 3. The AMM makes trades and incurs positive 𝖫𝖵𝖧\mathsf{LVH} on each individual time step: 𝖫𝖵𝖧0,1>0\mathsf{LVH}_{0,1}>0 and 𝖫𝖵𝖧1,2>0\mathsf{LVH}_{1,2}>0. However, the t=2t=2 portfolio is equal to the t=0t=0 portfolio so we have 𝖫𝖵𝖧0,2=0\mathsf{LVH}_{0,2}=0! The econometrician faces a paradox: the AMM appears to suffer positive losses at each individual time step, but no loss over the interval as a whole. Relatedly, 𝖫𝖵𝖧\mathsf{LVH} is not monotonic: adverse selection costs may appear to reverse as prices reconverge, even though the AMM has incurred genuine adverse selection costs at every step. By contrast, 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR} is monotonically non-decreasing, reflecting the economically natural property that adverse selection costs accumulate irreversibly over time.

Second, the sign of the change in 𝖫𝖵𝖧\mathsf{LVH} can vary, depending on the start point chosen. Consider an AMM with a fixed level of liquidity; suppose the AMM holds x=100x=100 of the risky asset at t1t_{1}, and x=200x=200 at t2t_{2}. Consider a future time period [t3,t4]\left[t_{3},t_{4}\right] during which holdings increase from 150 to 160. Then:

𝖫𝖵𝖧t1,t4−𝖫𝖵𝖧t1,t3<0\mathsf{LVH}_{t_{1},t_{4}}-\mathsf{LVH}_{t_{1},t_{3}}<0
𝖫𝖵𝖧t2,t4−𝖫𝖵𝖧t2,t3>0\mathsf{LVH}_{t_{2},t_{4}}-\mathsf{LVH}_{t_{2},t_{3}}>0

That is, 𝖫𝖵𝖧\mathsf{LVH} seems to increase relative to the t1t_{1} benchmark, but decrease relative to the t2t_{2} benchmark! Both interpretations are internally consistent; however, the econometrician cannot unambiguously conclude whether, in the time period [t3,t4]\left[t_{3},t_{4}\right], the AMM made or lost money. The magnitude, and even the sign, of the incremental profit depends on an arbitrarily chosen reference point.

Third, 𝖫𝖵𝖧\mathsf{LVH} is path-independent: for any CFMM, 𝖫𝖵𝖧0,T\mathsf{LVH}_{0,T} depends only on the initial and final prices P0P_{0} and PTP_{T}, not on the path of prices between them. This is economically problematic, since adverse selection costs should naturally depend on the price path. An LP should lose more to informed trading during a period of high volatility than during a period of low volatility, even if prices start and end at the same levels. By contrast, 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR} is explicitly path-dependent: for a constant-product AMM, (27) shows that 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR} accumulates faster during high-volatility periods, consistent with the intuition that adverse selection is more costly when prices are more volatile.

Fourth, 𝖫𝖵𝖧\mathsf{LVH} conflates the ‘‘alpha-like’’ microstructural component of LP returns — adverse selection costs specific to the AMM’s market-making function — with the ‘‘beta-like’’ market risk arising from the AMM’s asset holdings. Because 𝖫𝖵𝖧\mathsf{LVH} benchmarks against fixed holdings, it accrues market risk as the AMM’s holdings diverge from the benchmark over time (cf. Corollary 1). As our empirical analysis in Section 7 shows, this beta-like component is orders of magnitude larger than the alpha-like component in variance terms, and can easily overwhelm any microstructural signal. 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR}, by contrast, cleanly separates these two forces: the rebalancing strategy absorbs all beta-like market risk, isolating the alpha-like microstructural component of LP returns.

A natural way to fix these problems is to re-benchmark performance in each short time interval against holdings at the start of that interval. Fixing some period length Δ\Delta, we could define a loss metric LL, as:

Lt1,t2≜𝖫𝖵𝖧t1,t1+Δ+𝖫𝖵𝖧t1+Δ,t1+2​Δ+…+𝖫𝖵𝖧t2−Δ,t2L_{t_{1},t_{2}}\triangleq\mathsf{LVH}_{t_{1},t_{1}+\Delta}+\mathsf{LVH}_{t_{1}+\Delta,t_{1}+2\Delta}+\ldots+\mathsf{LVH}_{t_{2}-\Delta,t_{2}} (29)

That is, over each length-Δ\Delta interval, AMM payoffs are compared to holding the portfolio fixed at the beginning of that interval. This construction guarantees additivity:

Lt1,t2+Lt2,t3=Lt1,t3L_{t_{1},t_{2}}+L_{t_{2},t_{3}}=L_{t_{1},t_{3}} (30)

But (29) is exactly the definition of 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR}! Thus, 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR} can be thought of as simply a time-discretized, path-consistent version of 𝖫𝖵𝖧\mathsf{LVH}: it simply updates the benchmark portfolio at every interval as prices and holdings evolve.

8.2 ‘‘Impermanent Loss’’ in the Empirical AMM Literature

In the one-period models used in the majority of the theoretical literature on AMMs, ‘‘impermanent loss’’ has a simple and unambiguous interpretation. However, empiricists who wish to measure ‘‘impermanent loss’’ in practice must make an important measurement choice: whether to treat time as one long period, or several shorter periods.

In the absence of theoretical guidance, both choices have been made in the empirical literature. Augustin et al. (2024) appears to simply fix a start point and calculate impermanent loss based on holdings at that point in time.3030 30 Augustin et al. (2024) write: “The aggregate h-period return to yield farming is thus composed of four components associated with capital gains, impermanent losses, trading fees, and realized farm yields…” The following expression (8) then contains a difference of return metrics Rt,t+hAR_{t,t+h}^{A} and Rt,t+hBR_{t,t+h}^{B}, leading us to believe that the holdings are fixed at a start point tt, which appears to be set to September 23, 2020 for all pools. Other papers, such as Fang (2024) and Aquilina et al. (2024), appear to calculate impermanent loss on a number of shorter time intervals, and add the resulting losses up; specifically, we believe Aquilina et al. (2024) calculates impermanent loss using daily-updated holdings benchmarks,3131 31 On page 27, Aquilina et al. write: “We assess Fee Yield and Impermanent Loss on a daily basis, i.e. an LP can decide whether or not to provide liquidity at the end of each day”. and that the main specifications in Fang (2024) correspond to weekly-rebalanced impermanent loss.3232 32 Fang (2024) writes: “For the pool-level analyses, I aggregate transactions for each pool at daily, weekly, or monthly frequency. I focus on the weekly frequency because this appears to be the modal horizon for liquidity adjustment.” We note that (28) implies that there is no guarantee that daily-frequency losses thus calculated add up to weekly or monthly frequency results. Fang also writes: “Instead of loss-vs-holding, Milionis et al. (2022) show that LP returns can be characterized by loss-vsrebalancing (𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR}). My main results are qualitatively the same when using 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR}.” However, results using 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR} are not reported in the paper. This statement is plausible, since according to our definitions, the weekly-updated-holdings “impermanent loss” measure used in Fang (2024) calls is exactly equivalent to what we call “loss-versus-rebalancing”, rebalanced at a weekly frequency. Some papers, such as Heimbach et al. (2022), do not specify whether the holdings benchmark is updated periodically, or what the start point is.

All these papers refer to the object they measure as ‘‘impermanent loss’’, implicitly assuming that the underlying economic object measured is insensitive to these measurement decisions. This is incorrect. ‘‘Impermanent loss’’ measured using periodically updated holdings, versus fixed holdings, are substantively different metrics. The periodically-updated measure converges to fees minus adverse selection costs, for reasonably high update frequencies. The fixed-start-point measure, in our analysis in Section 7, has over a hundred times greater variance than the periodically-updated measure, and mainly reflects movements in ETH prices rather than any microstructural forces. The periodically-updated measure does not add up to the fixed-start measure, and the latter can easily be zero while the former is positive.

In our view, there is a missing link between the theoretical and empirical literature on AMMs: market risks are not salient in the one-period models used in most of the theoretical literature. As we showed in Figure 3, ‘‘impermanent loss’’ (loss versus holdings) and 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR} are identical over a single time step; the difference only emerges at the second step, where the AMM’s holdings deviate from the fixed-holding benchmark, and thus 𝖫𝖵𝖧\mathsf{LVH} begins to accrue market risk. This point has not been explicitly made in the theoretical AMM literature, allowing market risk to creep unnoticed into the metrics used in the empirical AMM literature. Our paper aims to fill this missing link: a simple dynamic model of AMMs allows us to clearly separate the distinct contributions of microstructural forces and market risk to AMM 𝖯&𝖫\mathsf{P\&L}.

Our paper gives clear guidance on how the empirical literature should proceed. If the goal of analysis is to measure microstructural effects — the performance of the AMM in its market-making capacity — the market-risk component of returns should be treated as a nuisance parameter to be eliminated, akin to how factor models are used to remove known sources of predictability from returns in equity-pricing settings. This can be done simply by subtracting the profits of the rebalancing strategy from pool 𝖯&𝖫\mathsf{P\&L}, as we do in Section 7. This is approximately the approach taken in Fang (2024) and Aquilina et al. (2024), though — aggressively extrapolating from our empirical analysis — both papers could benefit from slightly more frequent rebalancing, as we find that market risk still dominates microstructural forces at daily and weekly rebalancing frequencies. The loss measure obtained through this approach is mathematically and economically distinct from ‘‘impermanent loss’’ based on a fixed start point. We suggest, of course, calling this updated-holdings measure ‘‘loss versus rebalancing’’ instead of ‘‘impermanent loss’’.

Of course, different measures serve different purposes, and we cannot say in any formal sense that 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR} is the universally ‘‘best’’ metric. However, our model does suggest that fixed-start-point ‘‘impermanent loss’’ is simply equal to 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR}, plus the market risk exposures of a well-defined trading strategy, and the market risk component may be much larger than microstructural effects in variance terms. Thus, we believe papers which use fixed-start ‘‘impermanent loss’’ should make an argument for why it is appropriate to include this market risk, for the particular question they consider. As a minimum standard, papers should carefully specify the start-point and updating-frequency decisions they make in their implementation of metrics labelled ‘‘impermanent loss’’.

9 Option Pricing

We have shown that CFMM LPs behave like a bet on volatility, in the sense that 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR} is large when volatility is high. In this section, we briefly discuss the relationship of CFMM LPs to three classical and inter-related ways that volatility can be traded (Carr and Madan, 2001): static (European) options positions, dynamic trading strategies, and variance swaps. In Section B.1, we also demonstrate the equivalences between CFMM LP positions and these concepts in a simple two-step binomial tree model.

9.1 Static Options Positions

Our results are related to Clark (2020), Fukasawa et al. (2022), and Deng et al. (2023), who show that, over any finite time horizon, an AMM LP position’s payoff, ignoring fees, can be replicated by shorting a bundle of European options. Technically, this follows from the facts that the CFMM’s asset position and value are both path-independent: if the price is PTP_{T} at time TT, the CFMM holds x∗​(PT)x^{*}(P_{T}) of the risky asset and has pool value VT=V⁡(PT)V_{T}=V(P_{T}) corresponding to the final ‘‘payoff function’’ V⁡(⋅)V(\cdot), regardless of the path that prices took to reach PTP_{T}. More intuitively, at any time TT, the CFMM simply offers a menu of quantities of the asset to buy or sell at any given price, identically to a portfolio of European options. Ignoring fees, the CFMM exactly breaks even if prices do not move, PT=P0P_{T}=P_{0}, and loses money otherwise; hence, the CFMM LP position is essentially equivalent to giving away a bundle of European options. This intuition is consistent with the fact that the V⁡(⋅)V(\cdot) is a concave function (cf. Lemma 1).

Expected 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR} until period TT can be thought of as the value of the European options given away. This analogy gives another intuition for the comparative statics of expected 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR}. European options are worth more when volatility is higher, so 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR} is increasing in the volatility of the underlying asset. When the marginal liquidity of the AMM bonding curve is greater, the replicating portfolio of European options is larger: AMMs that trade more aggressively essentially give away more European options, also increasing 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR}.

As previous papers have discussed, the European option replication result also implies that, over any finite time horizon, the exposure of the AMM LP position to underlying prices can be totally hedged, by taking a long position in the replicating bundle of European options. This trade — a long position in the AMM LP, plus a short position in the replicating bundle of European options — is essentially a trading fee swap, betting on whether accrued trading fees from time 00 to TT are greater than European option premia of the replicating portfolio at time 00. The trader enters an LP position, and pays a premium for buying the replicating bundle of European options upfront. The AMM LP position then loses no money from price movements; the total position profits if the accrued trading fees until time TT are greater than the European option premia paid upfront, and loses otherwise.

9.2 Dynamic Trading Strategies

Classic options theory implies that static option positions are equivalent to dynamically trading the underlying asset in a certain way. The static option position is a combination of short straddles and strangles, selling out-of-money calls and puts. This position is equivalent to a dynamic trading strategy which sells the asset when prices increase, and buys when prices decrease. This is exactly what the AMM LP position does: observe that, from Lemma 1 Part 3, x∗​(⋅)x^{*}(\cdot) is non-increasing. If prices decrease slightly from P0P_{0} to Pt<P0P_{t}<P_{0}, the rebalancing strategy responds by buying the risky asset. The rebalancing strategy thus makes a profit, relative to simply holding the initial position x∗​(P0)x^{*}\left(P_{0}\right), if prices increase back to P0P_{0}, and makes a loss if prices decrease further from PtP_{t}. This argument holds symmetrically for price decreases, implying that the rebalancing strategy makes losses if prices diverge from P0P_{0}, and profits when prices make small movements away from P0P_{0} and back. In the special case where the risky asset’s price is a random walk, the rebalancing strategy thus breaks even on average. In contrast, when prices move away from P0P_{0} and back, the CFMM reverts to the initial value V⁡(P0)V\left(P_{0}\right), exactly breaking even: there is no profit from price convergence, to offset the losses the CFMM makes when prices diverge from P0P_{0}.

9.3 Variance Swaps

Finally, as discussed by Fukasawa et al. (2022), variance can be traded directly by trading swaps on realized variance. The VIX is such a contract, operating on a fixed finite time horizon. Applying Lemma 1 Part 3, the instantaneous 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR} of (8) can be re-written as

ℓ⁡(σ,P)=12×(σ​P)2×|x∗⁣′​(P)|.\ell(\sigma,P)=\tfrac{1}{2}\times(\sigma P)^{2}\times|x^{*\prime}(P)|.

Here, the first component, (σ​P)2(\sigma P)^{2}, is the instantaneous variance or quadratic variation of the price, i.e., for small Δ​t\Delta t, Var⁡[Pt+Δ​t|Pt=P]≈(σ​P)2​Δ​t\Var[P_{t+\Delta t}|P_{t}=P]\approx(\sigma P)^{2}\,\Delta t. Recalling that x∗​(P)x^{*}(P) is the total quantity of risky asset held by the pool if the price is PP, the second component, |x∗⁣′​(P)||x^{*\prime}(P)| corresponds to the marginal liquidity available from the pool at price level PP. Now, integrating over time, we have that

𝖫𝖵𝖱t=12​∫0t(σs​Ps)2×|x∗⁣′​(Ps)|​𝑑s=12​∫0t|x∗⁣′​(Ps)|​d​[P]s,∀t≥0.\mathsf{LVR}_{t}=\tfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{t}(\sigma_{s}P_{s})^{2}\times|x^{*\prime}(P_{s})|\,ds=\tfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{t}|x^{*\prime}(P_{s})|\,d[P]_{s},\quad\forall\ t\geq 0.

This expression is the payoff of the floating leg of a continuously sampled generalized variance swap (Carr and Lee, 2009, see, e.g.,), specifically a price variance swap that is weighted by marginal liquidity.

10 Discussion and Implications

Besides their positive value for understanding and quantifying the losses from AMM LPing, our results also suggest ways that these losses could be reduced or eliminated. We showed that CFMM LPs lose money from price slippage: when CEX prices move, CFMM quotes become ‘‘stale’’ and are vulnerable to sniping by rebalancing arbitrageurs. This slippage can in principle be eliminated: if an AMM had access to a high-frequency oracle for the CEX price PtP_{t}, the AMM could in principle quote prices arbitrarily close to PtP_{t}, up to the desired asset position x∗​(Pt)x^{*}\left(P_{t}\right).3333 33 A similar design is proposed in Krishnamachari et al. (2021b). Quoting prices this way would reduce arbitrageurs’ profits, allowing the AMM to achieve a payoff arbitrarily close to that of the rebalancing strategy. This design has a number of risks — it relies heavily on the accuracy of the oracle for PtP_{t}, and leaves open the potential for oracle manipulation — but in principle an oracle-based AMM could substantially reduce or eliminate 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR}.

A related set of AMM designs revolve around selling the right to arbitrage the pool to certain special wallets, and redistributing profits to AMM LPs. This could be done in several ways. Suppose a particular crypto wallet address, which we call the ‘‘authorized participant’’ or AP, had the unique right for the first AMM trade in every block. This first execution right effectively conveys the right to arbitrage the pool (Josojo, 2022). Alternatively, the AP could be provided the right to trade with the AMM paying zero fees (Jump Crypto, 2022). The AP would then have a large advantage in arbitrage trading, since the AP could profitably trade against arbitrarily small price movements, whereas prices would have to move at least as much as the AMM’s percentage trading fees for non-AP wallets to profit from arbitrage trade. The AP would thus be able to capture a large fraction of fees from arbitrage trade. In either of these designs, an AMM protocol aiming to reduce 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR} could thus run an AP wallet itself, doing CEX-DEX arbitrage, and redistributing arbitrage profits to LPs. Alternatively, AMM protocols could simply run periodic auctions — over longer periods, such as weeks or months — in which wallets can bid for the right to be authorized participants for some period of time. In principle, potential arbitrageurs should bid the ex ante expectation of arbitrage profits, which includes 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR}; the protocol can then redistribute these profits to LPs. Adams et al. (2024) analyzes this design in detail.3434 34 Note that one subtlety about the zero fee design is that, in addition to rebalancing arbitrage profits, APs would be able to capture reversion arbitrage profits; hence, 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR} provides a lower bound for how much revenue wallets could capture from having preferential access to arbitrage the pool. Both these methods capture either 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR} or its expectation, and redistribute the profits to pool LPs. Another strand of work has argued that 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR} would be reduced or eliminated if orders were sold in batch auctions, rather than placed directly in mempools; this design is discussed in Ramseyer et al. (2022) and Canidio and Fritsch (2023), and related ‘‘request-for-quotes’’ mechanisms are now in use in a number of widely used protocols.3535 35 “Batching” is used in CoWswap; a number of AMM protocols have also implemented related RFQ-like systems, such as Uniswap X, 1inch fusion, and Paraswap AugustusRFQ. We believe that these are interesting directions for future AMM design research.

An earlier line of work seeks to design specific CFMMs with good properties by identifying good bonding functions (Port and Tiruviluamala, 2022; Wu and McTighe, 2022; Forgy and Lau, 2021; Krishnamachari et al., 2021a). Our work suggests that bonding functions only affect 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR} insofar as they change the marginal liquidity of CFMMs. In certain cases, it may be desirable for marginal liquidity to vary with prices in a systematic way — this may be the case, for example, for stablecoin swap pairs. In other cases, different bonding functions, or ‘‘universal’’ AMM designs such as Uniswap v3, have equivalent infinitesimal 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR} whenever they have equivalent amounts of marginal liquidity for an asset pair.

11 Conclusion

Automated market makers are decentralized market makers. Market participants can both trade with AMMs, and contribute capital to participate in the liquidity provision activities of the AMM. In the second case, the AMM behaves essentially as an investment, similar to mutual funds or ETFs in traditional financial markets. In this paper, we have constructed a framework for understanding the returns to investments in AMM LP positions. We provide a simple model, in which LP 𝖯&𝖫\mathsf{P\&L} cleanly decomposes into a ‘‘beta-like’’ component reflecting market risk, and an ‘‘alpha-like’’ component reflecting the microstructural forces of fee revenue versus adverse selection losses. These components are straightforward to separate empirically: the beta component can be eliminated simply by subtracting the profits of the rebalancing strategy from LP 𝖯&𝖫\mathsf{P\&L}. Our results have implications for how to measure the returns to LP positions as investments.

Appendix

Appendix A Proofs

A.1 Proof of Lemma 1

The first part follows from the fact that 𝒞⊂ℝ+2\mathcal{C}\subset\mathbb{R}_{+}^{2} and P≥0P\geq 0. The second part is the envelope theorem or Danskin’s theorem (Bertsekas, 1971). The third part follows from the concavity of V⁡(⋅)V(\cdot), as a pointwise minimum of a collection of affine functions.

A.2 Proof of Lemma 2

First, we show that 𝖫𝖵𝖱t\mathsf{LVR}_{t} is equal to expression (7). The smoothness condition of 1 Part 2 allows us to apply Itô’s lemma to V⁡(⋅)V(\cdot) to obtain

d​Vt=V′​(Pt)​d​Pt+12​V′′​(Pt)​(d​Pt)2=V′​(Pt)​d​Pt+12​V′′​(Pt)​σ2​Pt2​d​t=x∗​(Pt)​d​Pt+12​V′′​(Pt)​σ2​Pt2​d​t,\begin{split}dV_{t}&=V^{\prime}(P_{t})\,dP_{t}+\tfrac{1}{2}V^{\prime\prime}(P_{t})\left(dP_{t}\right)^{2}\\ &=V^{\prime}(P_{t})\,dP_{t}+\tfrac{1}{2}V^{\prime\prime}(P_{t})\,\sigma^{2}P_{t}^{2}\,dt\\ &=x^{*}(P_{t})\,dP_{t}+\tfrac{1}{2}V^{\prime\prime}(P_{t})\,\sigma^{2}P_{t}^{2}\,dt,\end{split} (31)

where the last step follows from Lemma 1 Part 2. Comparing with (5), we obtain (7). Finally, the fact that ℓ⁡(σ,P)≥0\ell(\sigma,P)\geq 0 follows from Lemma 1 Part 3.

Next, we show that the cumulative profits of rebalancing arbitrageurs over the time interval [0,T][0,T] is equal to 𝖫𝖵𝖱T\mathsf{LVR}_{T}. We start with a discrete approximation to the arbitrage profit, indexed by N≥1N\geq 1. Suppose arbitrageurs arrive sequentially, so that the iith arbitrageur arrives at time τi\tau_{i}, for 1≤i≤N1\leq i\leq N. For convenience, set τ0≜0\tau_{0}\triangleq 0 and τN+1≜T\tau_{N+1}\triangleq T. For each 1≤i≤N1\leq i\leq N, at time τi\tau_{i}, the iith arbitrageur observes the price PτiP_{\tau_{i}}, rebalances the pool from (x∗​(Pτi−1),y∗​(Pτi−1))\big(x^{*}(P_{\tau_{i-1}}),y^{*}(P_{\tau_{i-1}})\big) to (x∗​(Pτi),y∗​(Pτi))\big(x^{*}(P_{\tau_{i}}),y^{*}(P_{\tau_{i}})\big). In other words, the arbitrageur purchases x∗​(Pτi−1)−x∗​(Pτi)x^{*}(P_{\tau_{i-1}})-x^{*}(P_{\tau_{i}}) units of the risky asset from the CFMM at average price :

Pi𝖢𝖥𝖬𝖬≜−y∗​(Pτi)−y∗​(Pτi−1)x∗​(Pτi)−x∗​(Pτi−1).P_{i}^{\mathsf{CFMM}}\triangleq-\frac{y^{*}(P_{\tau_{i}})-y^{*}(P_{\tau_{i-1}})}{x^{*}(P_{\tau_{i}})-x^{*}(P_{\tau_{i-1}})}.

The arbitrageur can then sell these units on the external market at price PτiP_{\tau_{i}} and earn profits (in the numéraire) from the difference in price according to

(Pτi−Pi𝖢𝖥𝖬𝖬)​[x∗​(Pτi−1)−x∗​(Pτi)]=Pτi​[x∗​(Pτi−1)−x∗​(Pτi)]+[y∗​(Pτi−1)−y∗​(Pτi)].\left(P_{\tau_{i}}-P_{i}^{\mathsf{CFMM}}\right)\left[x^{*}(P_{\tau_{i-1}})-x^{*}(P_{\tau_{i}})\right]=P_{\tau_{i}}\left[x^{*}(P_{\tau_{i-1}})-x^{*}(P_{\tau_{i}})\right]+\left[y^{*}(P_{\tau_{i-1}})-y^{*}(P_{\tau_{i}})\right].

Denote by 𝖠𝖱𝖡T(N)\mathsf{ARB}_{T}^{(N)} the aggregate arbitrage profits. Summing over 1≤i≤N1\leq i\leq N, telescoping the sum, and applying summation-by-parts yields

𝖠𝖱𝖡T(N)≜∑i=1N{Pτi​[x∗​(Pτi−1)−x∗​(Pτi)]+[y∗​(Pτi−1)−y∗​(Pτi)]}=∑i=1NPτi​[x∗​(Pτi−1)−x∗​(Pτi)]+y∗​(P0)−y∗​(PτN)=P0​x∗​(P0)+y∗​(P0)+∑i=0Nx∗​(Pτi)​[Pτi+1−Pτi]−PT​x∗​(PτN)−y∗​(PτN).\begin{split}\mathsf{ARB}_{T}^{(N)}&\triangleq\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left\{P_{\tau_{i}}\left[x^{*}(P_{\tau_{i-1}})-x^{*}(P_{\tau_{i}})\right]+\left[y^{*}(P_{\tau_{i-1}})-y^{*}(P_{\tau_{i}})\right]\right\}\\ &=\sum_{i=1}^{N}P_{\tau_{i}}\left[x^{*}(P_{\tau_{i-1}})-x^{*}(P_{\tau_{i}})\right]+y^{*}(P_{0})-y^{*}(P_{\tau_{N}})\\ &=P_{0}x^{*}(P_{0})+y^{*}(P_{0})+\sum_{i=0}^{N}x^{*}(P_{\tau_{i}})\left[P_{\tau_{i+1}}-P_{\tau_{i}}\right]-P_{T}x^{*}(P_{\tau_{N}})-y^{*}(P_{\tau_{N}}).\end{split}

Observe that the sum in the final expression is the discrete approximation of an Itô integral. Assume that the time partition mesh over [0,T][0,T] shrinks to zero as N→∞N\rightarrow\infty. Taking the limit as N→∞N\rightarrow\infty and passing to continuous time, the sum converges to an Itô integral, which is well-defined under 1 Part 3. Further, τN→T\tau_{N}\rightarrow T, so that PτN→PTP_{\tau_{N}}\rightarrow P_{T}, and x∗​(PτN)→x∗​(PT)x^{*}(P_{\tau_{N}})\rightarrow x^{*}(P_{T}), y∗​(PτN)→y∗​(PT)y^{*}(P_{\tau_{N}})\rightarrow y^{*}(P_{T}). Thus, it holds that

𝖠𝖱𝖡T≜limN→∞𝖠𝖱𝖡T(N)=V⁡(P0)+∫0Tx∗​(Pt)​d​Pt−V⁡(PT).\mathsf{ARB}_{T}\triangleq\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}\mathsf{ARB}_{T}^{(N)}=V(P_{0})+\int_{0}^{T}x^{*}(P_{t})\,dP_{t}-V(P_{T}).

Hence, the cumulative profits of rebalancing arbitrageurs from time 00 to time TT are equal to 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR}, defined in (6).

A.3 LVR, Marginal Liquidity, and Bonding Function Curvature

For sufficiently smooth CFMM bonding functions, the marginal liquidity can be expressed in terms of derivatives of the CFMM bonding function:

d​xd​P=∂f∂y(∂2f∂x2+P2​∂2f∂y2−2​P​∂2f∂x​∂y)\frac{dx}{dP}=\frac{\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}}{\left(\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x^{2}}+P^{2}\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial y^{2}}-2P\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x\partial y}\right)} (32)

Qualitatively, (32) implies that marginal liquidity, x′​(P)x^{\prime}\left(P\right), is related to the curvature of the CFMM invariant curves. The denominator of (32) is equal to P2P^{2} times the negative of the determinant of the bordered Hessian of ff. ff is strictly quasiconcave — that is, the upper level sets of ff are convex — if and only if this determinant is positive; moreover, the magnitude of the determinant is related to the curvature of the level curves of ff (Simon et al., 1994, p. 542). Thus, CFMM invariants with ‘‘flatter’’, more linear level curves will have greater marginal liquidity d​xd​P\frac{dx}{dP}, and also greater 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR}.

(32) is also useful because it can be used to calculate d​xd​P\frac{dx}{dP} using analytic expressions for bonding functions, which may be useful for computing 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR} in practice.

A.3.1 Derivation of (32)

The Lagrangian of the pool expenditure minimization problem, (1), is:

Λ=P​x+y+λ⁡[f⁡(x,y)−L]\Lambda=Px+y+\lambda\left[f\left(x,y\right)-L\right]

The optimal solution is characterized by the FOCs:

∂Λ∂x:P+λ​∂f∂x=0\frac{\partial\Lambda}{\partial x}:\ P+\lambda\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}=0 (33)
∂Λ∂y: 1+λ​∂f∂y=0\frac{\partial\Lambda}{\partial y}:\ 1+\lambda\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=0 (34)
∂Λ∂λ:f⁡(x,y)−L=0\frac{\partial\Lambda}{\partial\lambda}:\ f\left(x,y\right)-L=0 (35)

Now, we will take d​xd​P\frac{dx}{dP} by applying the implicit function theorem to this system of first-order conditions. The derivatives of the FOCs are:

∂∂P​∂Λ∂x: 1\frac{\partial}{\partial P}\frac{\partial\Lambda}{\partial x}:\ 1
∂∂P​∂Λ∂y: 0\frac{\partial}{\partial P}\frac{\partial\Lambda}{\partial y}:\ 0
∂∂P​∂Λ∂λ: 0\frac{\partial}{\partial P}\frac{\partial\Lambda}{\partial\lambda}:\ 0
∂∂x​∂Λ∂x:λ​∂2f∂x2\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\frac{\partial\Lambda}{\partial x}:\ \lambda\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x^{2}}
∂∂x​∂Λ∂y:λ​∂2f∂x​∂y\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\frac{\partial\Lambda}{\partial y}:\ \lambda\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x\partial y}
∂∂x​∂Λ∂λ:∂f∂x\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\frac{\partial\Lambda}{\partial\lambda}:\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}
∂∂y​∂Λ∂x:λ​∂2f∂x​∂y\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\frac{\partial\Lambda}{\partial x}:\ \lambda\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x\partial y}
∂∂y​∂Λ∂y:λ​∂2f∂y2\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\frac{\partial\Lambda}{\partial y}:\ \lambda\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial y^{2}}
∂∂y​∂Λ∂λ:∂f∂y\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\frac{\partial\Lambda}{\partial\lambda}:\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}
∂∂λ​∂Λ∂x:−∂f∂x\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda}\frac{\partial\Lambda}{\partial x}:\ -\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}
∂∂λ​∂Λ∂y:−∂f∂y\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda}\frac{\partial\Lambda}{\partial y}:\ -\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}
∂∂λ​∂Λ∂λ: 0\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda}\frac{\partial\Lambda}{\partial\lambda}:\ 0

Hence, we wish to solve the following system of equations for d​xd​P\frac{dx}{dP}:

∂∂P​∂Λ∂x+∂∂x​∂Λ∂x​d​xd​P+∂∂y​∂Λ∂x​d​yd​P+∂∂λ​∂Λ∂x​d​λd​P=0\frac{\partial}{\partial P}\frac{\partial\Lambda}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\frac{\partial\Lambda}{\partial x}\frac{dx}{dP}+\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\frac{\partial\Lambda}{\partial x}\frac{dy}{dP}+\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda}\frac{\partial\Lambda}{\partial x}\frac{d\lambda}{dP}=0
∂∂P​∂Λ∂y+∂∂x​∂Λ∂y​d​xd​P+∂∂y​∂Λ∂y​d​yd​P+∂∂λ​∂Λ∂y​d​λd​P=0\frac{\partial}{\partial P}\frac{\partial\Lambda}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\frac{\partial\Lambda}{\partial y}\frac{dx}{dP}+\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\frac{\partial\Lambda}{\partial y}\frac{dy}{dP}+\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda}\frac{\partial\Lambda}{\partial y}\frac{d\lambda}{dP}=0
∂∂P​∂Λ∂λ+∂∂x​∂Λ∂λ​d​xd​P+∂∂y​∂Λ∂λ​d​yd​P+∂∂λ​∂Λ∂λ​d​λd​P=0\frac{\partial}{\partial P}\frac{\partial\Lambda}{\partial\lambda}+\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\frac{\partial\Lambda}{\partial\lambda}\frac{dx}{dP}+\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\frac{\partial\Lambda}{\partial\lambda}\frac{dy}{dP}+\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda}\frac{\partial\Lambda}{\partial\lambda}\frac{d\lambda}{dP}=0

Substituting, we have:

1+λ​∂2f∂x2​d​xd​P+λ​∂2f∂x​∂y​d​yd​P−∂f∂x​d​λd​P=01+\lambda\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x^{2}}\frac{dx}{dP}+\lambda\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x\partial y}\frac{dy}{dP}-\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\frac{d\lambda}{dP}=0 (36)
0+λ​∂2f∂x​∂y​d​xd​P+λ​∂2f∂y2​d​yd​P−∂f∂y​d​λd​P=00+\lambda\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x\partial y}\frac{dx}{dP}+\lambda\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial y^{2}}\frac{dy}{dP}-\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\frac{d\lambda}{dP}=0 (37)
∂f∂x​d​xd​P+∂f∂y​d​yd​P=0\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\frac{dx}{dP}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\frac{dy}{dP}=0 (38)

Now, applying (33) and (34), we have:

∂f∂x=P​∂f∂y\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}=P\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} (39)

Thus, we can simplify (38) to:

d​yd​P=−P​d​xd​P\frac{dy}{dP}=-P\frac{dx}{dP}

Substituting into (36) and (37), we have:

1+λ​∂2f∂x2​d​xd​P+λ​∂2f∂x​∂y​(−P​d​xd​P)−∂f∂x​d​λd​P=01+\lambda\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x^{2}}\frac{dx}{dP}+\lambda\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x\partial y}\left(-P\frac{dx}{dP}\right)-\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\frac{d\lambda}{dP}=0
0+λ​∂2f∂x​∂y​d​xd​P+λ​∂2f∂y2​(−P​d​xd​P)−∂f∂y​d​λd​P=00+\lambda\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x\partial y}\frac{dx}{dP}+\lambda\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial y^{2}}\left(-P\frac{dx}{dP}\right)-\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\frac{d\lambda}{dP}=0

Rearranging,

(∂2f∂x2−P​∂2f∂x​∂y)​λ​d​xd​P=∂f∂x​d​λd​P−1\left(\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x^{2}}-P\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x\partial y}\right)\lambda\frac{dx}{dP}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\frac{d\lambda}{dP}-1 (40)
(∂2f∂x​∂y−P​∂2f∂y2)​λ​d​xd​P=∂f∂y​d​λd​P\left(\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x\partial y}-P\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial y^{2}}\right)\lambda\frac{dx}{dP}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\frac{d\lambda}{dP} (41)

Now, multiply (41) by PP, applying (39), and subtract (40), to get:

(∂2f∂x2+P2​∂2f∂y2−2​P​∂2f∂x​∂y)​λ​d​xd​P=−1\left(\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x^{2}}+P^{2}\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial y^{2}}-2P\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x\partial y}\right)\lambda\frac{dx}{dP}=-1

Now,

d​xd​P=−1λ⁡(∂2f∂x2+P2​∂2f∂y2−2​P​∂2f∂x​∂y)\frac{dx}{dP}=\frac{-1}{\lambda\left(\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x^{2}}+P^{2}\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial y^{2}}-2P\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x\partial y}\right)}

Now, to solve for λ\lambda, we simply use (34). Hence, we have:

d​xd​P=∂f∂y(∂2f∂x2+P2​∂2f∂y2−2​P​∂2f∂x​∂y)\frac{dx}{dP}=\frac{\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}}{\left(\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x^{2}}+P^{2}\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial y^{2}}-2P\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x\partial y}\right)} (42)

This is (32).

Appendix B Other Results

B.1 LVR and Impermanent Loss in a Two-Step Binomial Tree

Relationships to option strategies. The binomial tree example also helps illustrate the analogy between CFMM LP payoffs and European options. The time-2 difference between the payoffs of the rebalancing strategy and the buy-and-hold strategy is positive when prices mean-revert, and negative when prices diverge. Hence, payoffs are similar to those of a short European straddle or strangle position, which involves selling calls and puts which expire after two periods. The positive payoff when prices revert can be thought of as the option premia collected from selling the straddle, and the negative payoffs when prices diverge can be thought of as the payouts to the option buyer, which are made if either the call or the put sold expire in-the-money. The CFMM LP position has a similar pattern of payoffs, but makes 0 profits if prices end where they started. An CFMM LP position, ignoring fees, can thus be thought of like giving away a straddle position, without collecting any upfront option premia. Viewed this way, the equivalence between the rebalancing strategy and the static European strangle on the binomial tree reflects the classic idea that static option positions can be replicated by dynamically trading the underlying asset; in this case, European straddles and strangles are replicated by a strategy which sells the risky asset when prices increase and buys when prices decrease.

B.2 Weighted Geometric Mean Market Makers

Weighted geometric mean market makers have the special property that the instantaneous 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR} per dollar of pool value, i.e., ℓ⁡(σ,P)/V⁡(P)\ell(\sigma,P)/V(P), is a constant. The following theorem establishes that these are essentially the only CFMMs for which this is true:

2.

Suppose a CFMM satisfies

ℓ⁡(σ,P)V⁡(P)=c⁡(σ),∀P≥0.\frac{\ell(\sigma,P)}{V(P)}=c(\sigma),\quad\forall\ P\geq 0. (43)

Then, we have

V⁡(P)=L1​Pθ⁡(σ)+L2​P1−θ⁡(σ),V(P)=L_{1}P^{\theta(\sigma)}+L_{2}P^{1-\theta(\sigma)}, (44)

for free constants L1,L2≥0L_{1},L_{2}\geq 0, where

θ⁡(σ)≜1−1−8​c​(σ)/σ22≤12.\theta(\sigma)\triangleq\frac{1-\sqrt{1-8c(\sigma)/\sigma^{2}}}{2}\leq\frac{1}{2}.

Comparing with Example 2, observe that (44) states that the pool can only be the ‘‘sum’’ of θ\theta and 1−θ1-\theta weighted geometric mean market makers. The two degrees of freedom are intuitive, since θ\theta and 1−θ1-\theta are exchangeable in (18).

Proof of Theorem 2.

We construct the following ODE from the (43) along with (8),

P2​V′′​(P)+c¯​V​(P)=0,P^{2}V^{\prime\prime}(P)+\bar{c}V(P)=0,

with constant c¯≜2​c/σ2\bar{c}\triangleq 2c/\sigma^{2}. Make the substitution P=ezP=e^{z}, to arrive at the equivalent ODE,

V′′​(z)−V′​(z)+c¯​V​(z)=0,V^{\prime\prime}(z)-V^{\prime}(z)+\bar{c}V(z)=0,

which when solved, along with the known limit condition from (1) that V⁡(z)→0V(z)\rightarrow 0 as z→−∞z\to-\infty, by the usual method of linear ODEs results in the generic solution,

V⁡(P)=L1​P1−1−4​c¯2+L2​P1+1−4​c¯2=L1​Pθ+L2​P1−θ.V(P)=L_{1}P^{\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4\bar{c}}}{2}}+L_{2}P^{\frac{1+\sqrt{1-4\bar{c}}}{2}}=L_{1}P^{\theta}+L_{2}P^{1-\theta}.

Note that the above calculation is allowed because the quantity under the root is necessarily non-negative, as if it were not, then V⁡(P)V(P) would not be everywhere concave, which must be the case by Lemma 1. ∎

B.3 Multi-Dimensional Generalization

In this section, we describe the multi-dimensional generalization of our results. Specifically, denote by vectors x∈ℝ+nx\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n} the reserves in n≥2n\geq 2 assets (none of which need be the numéraire), and Pt∈ℝ+nP_{t}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n} a vector of prices (in terms of the numéraire). We assume that the price vector evolves according to geometric Brownian motion, i.e.,

d​Pt=diag⁡(Pt)​Σt1/2​d​Btℚ,∀t≥0,dP_{t}=\diag(P_{t})\Sigma_{t}^{1/2}\,dB_{t}^{\mathbb{Q}},\quad\forall\ t\geq 0,

with covariance matrix of returns Σt∈ℝn×n\Sigma_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, Σt⪰0\Sigma_{t}\succeq 0, and where BtℚB_{t}^{\mathbb{Q}} is a standard ℚ\mathbb{Q}-Brownian motion on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}.

Given a bonding function f:ℝ+n→ℝf\colon\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}, define the pool value function V:ℝ+n→ℝ+V\colon\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+} according to

V⁡(P)≜minimizex∈ℝ+nP⊤​xsubject tof⁡(x)=L.\begin{array}[]{lll}V(P)\triangleq&\mathop{\mathrm{minimize}}\limits_{x\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}}&P^{\top}x\\ &\text{\rm subject to}&f(x)=L.\end{array}

Analogous to 1, we will assume that an optimal solution x∗​(P)x^{*}(P) exists for all P∈ℝ+nP\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}, that V⁡(⋅)V(\cdot) is twice continuously differentiable, and a suitable square-integrability condition on x∗​(⋅)x^{*}(\cdot).

Analogous to Lemma 1, we have

3.

For all prices P∈ℝ+nP\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}, the pool value function satisfies:

  1. 1.

    V⁡(P)≥0V(P)\geq 0.

  2. 2.

    ∇V​(P)=x∗​(P)≥0\nabla V(P)=x^{*}(P)\geq 0.

  3. 3.

    ∇2V​(P)=∇x∗​(P)⪯0\nabla^{2}V(P)=\nabla x^{*}(P)\preceq 0.

Define the rebalancing strategy by xt=x∗​(Pt)x_{t}=x^{*}(P_{t}), with value

Rt=V0+∫0tx∗​(Ps)⊤​d​Ps,∀t≥0.R_{t}=V_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}x^{*}(P_{s})^{\top}dP_{s},\quad\forall\ t\geq 0.

Then, we have the following multi-dimensional analog of Lemma 2:

3.

Loss-versus-rebalancing takes the form

𝖫𝖵𝖱t=∫0tℓ⁡(Σs,Ps)​𝑑s,∀t≥0,\mathsf{LVR}_{t}=\int_{0}^{t}\ell(\Sigma_{s},P_{s})\,ds,\quad\forall\ t\geq 0,

where we define, for P≥0P\geq 0, the instantaneous 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR}

ℓ(Σ,P)≜−12tr[diag(P)Σdiag(P)∇x∗(P)]≥0,\ell(\Sigma,P)\triangleq-\tfrac{1}{2}\tr\left[\diag(P)\Sigma\diag(P)\,\nabla x^{*}(P)\right]\geq 0,

where we have applied Lemma 3. In the case where Σ=σ2​I\Sigma=\sigma^{2}I, i.e., i.i.d. assets, we have that

ℓ(Σ,P)=−σ22tr[diag(P)2∇x∗(P)]=−σ22∑i=1nPi2∂∂Pix∗(P)≥0.\ell(\Sigma,P)=-\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2}\tr\left[\diag(P)^{2}\,\nabla x^{*}(P)\right]=-\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2}\ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\ P_{i}^{2}\frac{\partial}{\partial P_{i}}x^{*}(P)\geq 0.

In particular, 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR} is a non-negative, non-decreasing, and predictable process.

Proof.

Applying Itô’s lemma to Vt=V⁡(P)V_{t}=V(P),

d​Vt=∇V(Pt)⊤dPt+12(dPt)⊤∇2V(Pt)dPt=x∗​(Pt)⊤​d​Pt+12​tr​[Σt1/2​diag⁡(P)​∇2V​(Pt)​diag⁡(P)​Σt1/2]​d​t=d​Rt−ℓ⁡(Σt,Pt)​d​t.\begin{split}dV_{t}&=\nabla V(P_{t})^{\top}\,dP_{t}+\tfrac{1}{2}(dP_{t})^{\top}\nabla^{2}V(P_{t})\,dP_{t}\\ &=x^{*}(P_{t})^{\top}\,dP_{t}+\tfrac{1}{2}\tr\left[\Sigma_{t}^{1/2}\diag(P)\nabla^{2}V(P_{t})\diag(P)\Sigma_{t}^{1/2}\right]\,dt\\ &=dR_{t}-\ell(\Sigma_{t},P_{t})\,dt.\end{split}

Appendix C Data and Measurement

C.1 Data

Prices. We download minute-level USDC-ETH prices from the Binance API. We use close prices at the end of each minute for PtP_{t}.

Uniswap. We download data on the Uniswap v2 WETH-USDC pool from Dune Analytics, a data provider which aggregates data from the Ethereum blockchain into SQL databases. The queries we use to extract this data are included in Section C.2.

Mints and burns. In each minute, we observe the gross amounts of each asset in which are withdrawn through ‘‘burns’’, and deposited through ‘‘mints’’. Let (xtmint,ytmint)(x_{t}^{\text{mint}},y_{t}^{\text{mint}}) and (xtburn,ytburn)(x_{t}^{\text{burn}},y_{t}^{\text{burn}}) be the total amounts of each asset xx and yy which are minted and burned respectively, between time t−1t-1 and time tt. We will value minted and burned assets at the time-tt closing price PtP_{t}. Thus, the monetary value of mints and burns respectively are:

Πtmint≜ytmint+Pt​xtmint,Πtburn≜ytburn+Pt​xtburn.\Pi_{t}^{\text{mint}}\triangleq y_{t}^{\text{mint}}+P_{t}x_{t}^{\text{mint}},\quad\Pi_{t}^{\text{burn}}\triangleq y_{t}^{\text{burn}}+P_{t}x_{t}^{\text{burn}}.

Let (xt,yt)(x_{t},y_{t}) be the total asset holdings of the pool at time tt. As in the model, define the pool value at time tt by

Vt≜yt+Pt​xt.V_{t}\triangleq y_{t}+P_{t}x_{t}.

We can calculate Δ​LP 𝖯&𝖫t\Delta\text{LP\ $\mathsf{P\&L}_{t}$}, the change in 𝖯&𝖫\mathsf{P\&L} of the pool, from period t−1t-1 to tt, as

Δ​LP 𝖯&𝖫t≜Vt+Πtburn−Πtmint−Vt−1.\Delta\text{LP\ $\mathsf{P\&L}_{t}$}\triangleq V_{t}+\Pi_{t}^{\text{burn}}-\Pi_{t}^{\text{mint}}-V_{t-1}. (45)

In words, this is the value of pool reserves at time tt valued at price PtP_{t}, plus burned assets and minus minted assets valued at PtP_{t}, minus the value of pool reserves at time t−1t-1 valued at Pt−1P_{t-1}. Note that, in contrast to our simplifying assumption in the model that fees are paid in the numéraire, in practice in Uniswap v2 fees are paid directly into the pool reserves; hence, the pool 𝖯&𝖫\mathsf{P\&L} includes transaction fees paid into the pool.

Rebalancing strategy. We rebalance the pool at different time frequencies. For each rebalancing frequency, we compute the returns of a strategy which at any point in time holds as much ETH as the pool holds at the start of the period. For example, if the rebalancing frequency is daily, we set xtR​Bx_{t}^{RB} at any minute tt equal to the LP pool reserves at the start of the day containing the minute tt. We then calculate the returns on the rebalancing strategy using expression (26), that is:

Δ​RB 𝖯&𝖫t=xtR​B​(Pt+1−Pt).\Delta\text{RB\ $\mathsf{P\&L}_{t}$}=x_{t}^{RB}\left(P_{t+1}-P_{t}\right). (46)

Fees. In each minute, we compute the gross amount of each asset in the pair bought and sold. The Uniswap v2 pool has a fixed fee rate of 30bps on the contributed asset; we thus calculate fees in each asset by multiplying the gross amount contributed of each asset by 0.003. Call these fees xtf​e​ex_{t}^{fee} and ytf​e​ey_{t}^{fee} in period tt. We value fees at the period tt price; thus, the monetary value of fees in period tt, which we will call Δ​𝖥𝖤𝖤t\Delta\mathsf{FEE}_{t}, is:

Δ​𝖥𝖤𝖤t≜ytf​e​e+Pt​xtf​e​e.\Delta\mathsf{FEE}_{t}\triangleq y_{t}^{fee}+P_{t}x_{t}^{fee}. (47)

Note also that Uniswap v2 allows for ‘‘flash loans’’, in which assets are withdrawn and returned within a single transaction. Flash loans which are accounted for simply as swaps in Uniswap v2; thus, the calculation in (47) also correctly accounts for flash loans revenues.3636 36 See the Uniswap v2 documentation of flash swaps.

LVR. We compute a realized daily volatility using USDC-ETH prices from the Binance API sampled at 60 minute intervals. Let Δ​𝖫𝖵𝖱t\Delta\mathsf{LVR}_{t} be the increment of 𝖫𝖵𝖱\mathsf{LVR} in period tt. As in Example 3, we then calculate Δ​𝖫𝖵𝖱t\Delta\mathsf{LVR}_{t} simply as

Δ​𝖫𝖵𝖱t≜σ^t28×Vt×Δ​t,\Delta\mathsf{LVR}_{t}\triangleq\frac{\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{t}}{8}\times V_{t}\times\Delta t, (48)

where σ^t\hat{\sigma}_{t} denotes the realized daily volatilty estimate for the day containing period tt, and Δ​t=1/(24×60)\Delta t=1/(24\times 60) corresponds to a one minute period. This is a discrete approximation of (27).

Adding everything up. We then calculate the cumulative returns, the left side of (24), as:

LP 𝖯&𝖫 t−∫0tx∗​(Ps)​d​Ps≜∑t=1T(Δ​𝖯&𝖫t−Δ​RB 𝖯&𝖫t),\text{LP $\mathsf{P\&L}$ }_{t}-\int_{0}^{t}x^{*}(P_{s})\,dP_{s}\triangleq\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\Delta\mathsf{P\&L}_{t}-\Delta\text{RB\ $\mathsf{P\&L}_{t}$}\right),

using the definitions of Δ​LP 𝖯&𝖫t\Delta\text{LP\ $\mathsf{P\&L}_{t}$} and Δ​RB 𝖯&𝖫t\Delta\text{RB\ $\mathsf{P\&L}_{t}$} in (45) and (46) respectively. Note that different rebalancing frequencies give slightly different values of for Δ​RB 𝖯&𝖫t\Delta\text{RB\ $\mathsf{P\&L}_{t}$}. We calculate the right side of (24) as:

𝖥𝖤𝖤t−𝖫𝖵𝖱t≜∑t=1T(Δ​𝖥𝖤𝖤t−Δ​𝖫𝖵𝖱t),\mathsf{FEE}_{t}-\mathsf{LVR}_{t}\triangleq\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\Delta\mathsf{FEE}_{t}-\Delta\mathsf{LVR}_{t}\right),

using the definitions of Δ​𝖥𝖤𝖤t\Delta\mathsf{FEE}_{t} and Δ​𝖫𝖵𝖱t\Delta\mathsf{LVR}_{t} in (47) and (48) respectively.

C.2 Dune SQL Queries

This appendix contains the SQL queries we use on Dune to extract Uniswap v2 WETH-USDC data.

Mints.

⬇
1 SELECT to_char(evt_block_time, ’YYYY-MM-DD"T"HH24:MI:SSOF’) AS ts, *
2 FROM uniswap_v2."Pair_evt_Mint"
3 WHERE contract_address = ’\xb4e16d0168e52d35cacd2c6185b44281ec28c9dc’
4 ORDER BY evt_block_number, evt_index ASC

Burns.

⬇
1 SELECT to_char(evt_block_time, ’YYYY-MM-DD"T"HH24:MI:SSOF’) AS ts, *
2 FROM uniswap_v2."Pair_evt_Burn"
3 WHERE contract_address = ’\xb4e16d0168e52d35cacd2c6185b44281ec28c9dc’
4 ORDER BY evt_block_number, evt_index ASC

Trades.

⬇
1 SELECT
2 date_trunc(’minute’, evt_block_time) AS minute,
3 SUM("amount0In") as "amount0In",
4 SUM("amount1In") as "amount1In",
5 SUM("amount0Out") as "amount0Out",
6 SUM("amount1Out") as "amount1Out"
7 FROM uniswap_v2."Pair_evt_Swap"
8 WHERE contract_address = ’\xb4e16d0168e52d35cacd2c6185b44281ec28c9dc’
9 GROUP BY 1
10 ORDER BY 1 ASC

Pool reserves.

⬇
1 SELECT
2 minute,
3 latest_reserves[3] AS reserve0,
4 latest_reserves[4] AS reserve1
5 FROM
6 (SELECT date_trunc(’minute’, evt_block_time) AS minute,
7 (SELECT MAX(ARRAY[evt_block_number, evt_index, reserve0, reserve1]))
8 AS latest_reserves
9 FROM uniswap_v2."Pair_evt_Sync"
10 WHERE contract_address = ’\xb4e16d0168e52d35cacd2c6185b44281ec28c9dc’
11 GROUP BY 1) AS day_reserves
12 ORDER BY 1 ASC
